text.p: These are the main stories in Latvian newspapers on Wednesday. Prepared for Reuters by the Co-operation Fund. Reuters has not verified these reports and does not vouch for their accuracy:

- Deputy Janis Adamsons, who has proposed a parliamentary committee to investigate the activities of the Latvian Savings Bank and Unibanka, thinks that as a result of the investigation "somebody" will be brought to justice. It is not clear whether parliament will set up the commission.

- Parliament's committee for human rights and public affairs, the interior ministry and the president's office are drawing up an amnesty law. Some 20 percent of Latvia's 10,000 prison inmates will be subject to the amnesty.

- At the Lisbon OSCE conference, President Guntis Ulmanis said the functioning of the Skrunda radar station will expire in 1998 and it will have to be demolished. He called an anchievement the fact that no international organisation talks about the existence of a human rights problem in Latvia.
- Customs authorities in Riga are to confiscate some of the 2.15 million litres of alcohol seized by the British company Crown Agents, which is helping the Latvian Customs.

- Scandinavian ministers for immigration decided that their countries will provide asylum to 108 refugees from the refugee camp in Olaine. They said this was an extraordinary step and hoped that Latvian legislation will be brougt into line with the 1951 Convention on refugees.
- Judging by recent statements by Latvian officials, no radical turn is to be expected in talks on the Russian-Latvian border, the newsaper says.
- The creditors of Banka Baltija were unhappy with the auction that was held to sell off the bank's assets.
